Pipeline index
Compare the same assumptions across deals.
Use multi-deal-pipeline.csv for one property per row. Record your source and date for rent, taxes, insurance, and financing. Leave unknowns blank rather than treating them as zero.
Keep asking price separate from your proposed purchase price. Annualize rent, vacancy, expenses, debt service, and reserves consistently before comparing cash flow.
NOI = annual scheduled rent x (1 - vacancy rate) - annual operating expenses. Before-tax cash flow after reserves = NOI - annual debt service - annual capital reserve.

Market screening checklist
Collect evidence before selecting a neighborhood.
[ ] Define the geographic boundary, property type, and intended tenant use.
[ ] Record several comparable rentals with dates, condition, concessions, and time listed. Distinguish asking rents from signed lease evidence.
[ ] Research employment concentration, access to daily needs, and competing rental supply. Record sources; do not assume historical trends will continue.
[ ] Check local rental licensing, inspection, zoning, occupancy, and landlord requirements with official sources and qualified local counsel.
[ ] Obtain insurance indications and investigate flood, fire, storm, and other property-specific hazards.
[ ] Verify taxes and possible reassessment after purchase. Review utility responsibility, HOA restrictions, and special assessments.
[ ] Ask local managers about leasing time, service costs, tenant turnover, and operational constraints.

Conservative underwriting checklist
Make the assumptions visible and consistent.
[ ] Separate verified documents from estimates. Date every key input and record its source.
[ ] Use supportable monthly rent; include vacancy and collection loss. Do not treat a seller pro forma as a lease.
[ ] Include taxes, insurance, owner-paid utilities, management, routine repairs, HOA costs, licensing, and other recurring operating costs.
[ ] Include management cost even if initially self-managing. Keep capital replacements in a separate reserve to avoid hiding them.
[ ] NOI excludes loan payments, depreciation, income taxes, and capital expenditures. State your convention when comparing reports.
[ ] Use actual proposed principal-and-interest payments and financing fees. Do not count tax/insurance escrow twice.
[ ] Cash invested includes down payment, closing, initial rehab, and initial reserves; do not use down payment alone.
[ ] Test lower rent, higher vacancy, repairs, insurance changes, and financing changes. Identify the cash needed to cover shortfalls.
[ ] Confirm inspection, title, lease, insurance, and lender conditions before a commitment.

Appraisal prep checklist
Organize factual records without assuming a valuation outcome.
[ ] Ask the lender what documents may be submitted and how the appraisal process works.
[ ] Prepare a factual property summary with permitted use, layout, and verified measurements or source.
[ ] Gather permits, final approvals, dated before-and-after photos, and itemized completed work.
[ ] Keep receipts and paid invoices. Cost of work is not necessarily equal to added value.
[ ] Organize leases, rent roll, and operating records if requested by the lender or appraiser.
[ ] Identify relevant comparable properties with dates and differences; do not cherry-pick only the highest values.
[ ] Arrange authorized access, utilities, and safe inspection conditions.
[ ] Record unfinished work and material defects accurately. Never conceal adverse information.
[ ] Review the resulting report for factual errors through the lender’s process. Respect appraiser independence.
Refinance timeline checklist
Work backward from the loan maturity and your cash runway.
Target refinance date: ________   Existing loan maturity: ________   Cash runway: ________
Early planning: ask lenders about seasoning, title, occupancy, income coverage, loan size, and documentation requirements. Record requirements in writing.
Before rehab begins: confirm permits, scope, funding, and any completion conditions. Plan an exit that does not depend on a refinance.
During rehab: track costs and changes; retain paid invoices and inspection approvals. Update the cash runway.
Before application: assemble leases, insurance, financial records, entity/title documents, payoff details, and property information requested by the lender.
During underwriting: track appraisal, title, conditions, rate-lock terms, expiration dates, and any new cash requirement.
Before closing: review final loan terms, fees, prepayment provisions, cash to close, payment schedule, and reserve requirements with appropriate professionals.
After closing: reconcile proceeds and payoff; update debt service and reserve plans; calendar reporting and maturity dates.

Questions for a CPA
Bring records and questions, not an assumed tax outcome.
[ ] What records should I keep for this property, and how should ownership and activity be documented?
[ ] How should I distinguish repairs, improvements, acquisition costs, and financing costs in my records?
[ ] What information do you need to evaluate depreciation, placed-in-service dates, and land allocation?
[ ] Which limitations or classifications could affect the treatment of my rental activity in my circumstances?
[ ] What should I discuss with you before a refinance, ownership change, property sale, or exchange?
[ ] How should I track mixed personal/rental use, travel, management time, and shared expenses if relevant?
[ ] Are there federal, state, or local filing, withholding, or estimated-payment questions I should address?
[ ] What documents and deadlines should we plan for, and when should we revisit this review?
Records to bring: closing statements, leases, income/expense ledger, invoices, loan statements, prior returns, improvement history, and ownership documents as applicable.
